heroLead: Finleyville sits in some of the busiest Marcellus wet-gas acreage in the state, and families here have watched Range Resources drill this ground harder than almost anywhere else in Pennsylvania.
intro: Finleyville is a Washington County borough along PA-88 and Peters Creek, squarely inside the wet-gas core of the Marcellus play that's made this county one of the most heavily developed in the state. If your family has owned land here for a while, there's a good chance you've already got a lease, a division order, and a stack of royalty statements — and probably a lot of questions about the deductions on them.
We buy mineral and royalty interests around Finleyville, whether you're holding a producing interest with years of statements behind it or acreage that's leased but hasn't seen a rig yet.

sections.heading: Core wet-gas country
paragraphs: Washington County sits at the heart of the Marcellus wet-gas fairway, and Finleyville specifically has seen dense horizontal development from Range Resources and other operators for well over a decade. That density generally means stronger well performance history to evaluate, but it also means larger pooled units with more owners sharing a single well's production.

sections.heading: The deduction complaint we hear most in this county
paragraphs: Washington County royalty owners are some of the most vocal in the state about post-production deductions — gathering, compression, dehydration, marketing charges — eating into checks that started at a full 1/8 or better on paper. Pennsylvania's Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act sets a 1/8 floor, but the Kilmer v. Elexco decision left room for deductions to apply on top of that floor depending on lease language, and that's exactly the gap most Finleyville-area complaints fall into.

sections.heading: What we look at before making an offer
paragraphs: Well performance, decline curve, remaining lease term, and current market activity all factor into value here more than in less-developed counties, since there's usually real production history to review.

faqs.question: Why does Washington County see so much Marcellus activity around Finleyville?
faqs.answer: It sits in the wet-gas core of the play, where the shale is thick and liquids-rich, which has drawn dense horizontal development from Range Resources and other operators for over a decade.

faqs.question: My royalty check from a Finleyville-area well is smaller than my lease's stated percentage. Why?
faqs.answer: Almost always post-production deductions — gathering, compression, dehydration, and marketing costs the operator nets out before paying royalty, depending on lease wording. Pennsylvania law sets a 1/8 floor on gross royalty but doesn't ban these deductions outright.

faqs.question: Does a large pooled unit near Finleyville affect what my interest is worth?
faqs.answer: It can. A larger unit means more owners sharing one well's production, so your proportionate share and the unit's overall performance both matter to the value of your interest.
